lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.intro: Bowing is the standard Japanese greeting, and it shows up constantly — but you don't need to master it perfectly to be understood as polite.
lessons.didYouKnow: As a visitor, a small nod of the head is generally well received and not expected to match the precise depth/duration rules Japanese people learn — trying too hard to bow "correctly" is far less important than just being respectful.

phrases.text: ありがとうございます (Arigatou gozaimasu)

commonMistakes: Offering a handshake by default — a small bow or nod is more standard, though many Japanese people will happily shake hands with visitors too.

quiz.question: As a visitor, how much do you need to worry about bowing "correctly"?
options: It must be perfect or it's offensive
A small, respectful nod is well received
Bowing should never be attempted by visitors

lessons.title: Emergency Phrases
lessons.intro: Quick phrases worth having ready before you land — Japan has separate numbers for police and medical emergencies, unlike the single-number system in the EU.
lessons.didYouKnow: Japan uses 110 for police and 119 for fire/ambulance — there's no single unified emergency number like the EU's 112, so it's worth knowing which one you actually need.

phrases.text: 医者が必要です (Isha ga hitsuyou desu)

commonMistakes: Assuming one number covers everything like 911 — dial 119 for medical/fire, 110 for police.

quiz.question: Which number do you call for an ambulance in Japan?

lessons.title: Train Etiquette
lessons.intro: Japanese trains are famously punctual and quiet — the social norms on board are as important to know as the ticketing system itself.
lessons.didYouKnow: Taking phone calls on a train is considered quite rude — phones are kept on silent ("manner mode"), and texting/browsing quietly is fine, but voice calls are not.

phrases.text: この電車は〇〇に行きますか? (Kono densha wa 〇〇 ni ikimasu ka?)
phrases.pronunciation: koh-noh den-shah wah ___ nee ee-kee-mahs kah

commonMistakes: Taking a phone call on a train — step into the vestibule area between cars if you must, but a call in the main seating area draws real disapproval.
Eating a full meal on a regular commuter train — this is fine on long-distance Shinkansen but considered impolite on local trains.

quiz.question: What should you do with your phone on a Japanese train?
options: Keep it on silent, avoid voice calls

quiz.question: Is eating a full meal generally fine on a local commuter train?
options: No, it's seen as impolite (long-distance trains are different)

lessons.title: Dining Etiquette
lessons.intro: Japanese dining customs — especially around chopsticks and tipping — are easy to get wrong without knowing them, and locals will usually be too polite to correct you.
lessons.didYouKnow: Tipping is not customary in Japan and can even cause confusion or be politely refused — excellent service is simply the standard, not something that requires an extra payment to acknowledge.

phrases.text: ごちそうさまでした (Gochisousama deshita)
phrases.translation: Said after eating, thanking for the meal

commonMistakes: Sticking chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice — this resembles a funeral ritual and is considered inappropriate at a table.
Leaving a tip on the table — it's not expected and can create an awkward moment as staff may try to return it to you.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't you stick chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice?
Is tipping expected at Japanese restaurants?

lessons.title: Shopping Etiquette
lessons.intro: Japan still leans more on cash than many visitors expect, and there are a few small customs around paying that are worth knowing.
lessons.didYouKnow: Handing cash directly into a cashier's hand is unusual — most registers have a small tray for you to place money on, and change is returned to you the same way.

phrases.text: クレジットカードは使えますか? (Kurejitto kaado wa tsukaemasu ka?)
phrases.translation: Can I use a credit card?

commonMistakes: Assuming cards are accepted everywhere — many smaller shops, restaurants, and vending machines are still cash-only.
Handing cash directly to the cashier instead of using the small payment tray on the counter.

quiz.question: What's the small tray at many Japanese registers for?

lessons.title: Onsen Etiquette
lessons.intro: A hot spring bath ("onsen") is a classic Japanese experience — but it comes with strict etiquette that surprises most first-timers.
lessons.didYouKnow: You wash and rinse completely at the shower stations before ever entering the onsen water itself — the bath is for soaking, not washing, and skipping this step is considered a real breach of etiquette.

phrases.text: タトゥーがあります (Tatuu ga arimasu)

commonMistakes: Entering the onsen water without fully washing and rinsing first at the shower stations.
Bringing your towel into the water — it's meant to stay out of the bath, often folded on your head or set aside.

quiz.question: What should you do before entering the onsen water?
options: Fully wash and rinse at the shower stations first
Bring your towel in with you
